analysis.one_liner: Taxes windfall profits of large oil companies and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 19 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a 50% excise tax on the excess profits of large crude oil producers and importers — companies handling more than 300,000 barrels a day — charged only on oil profits above the average pre-pandemic Brent price of 2015-2019. The money would go into a fund and be rebated to individual taxpayers as a refundable credit, phasing out for households making over $150,000 a year, with larger rebates for joint filers. It would also apply retroactively to quarters in 2022, when oil company profits hit record highs after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers, especially middle- and lower-income households: the rebate is a fully refundable credit, so even families owing no income tax get paid, and it phases out only above $75,000 for singles and $150,000 for joint returns [S3]. It targets big oil's profits during price spikes — the companies that handle over 300,000 barrels a day — while exempting smaller producers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on large oil producers' and importers' windfall profits, charged only on the amount by which Brent crude prices exceed their 2015-2019 average, inflation-adjusted [S3].
Returns the full amount collected to individual taxpayers through a refundable gasoline price rebate credit, with joint filers receiving 150% of the single rate [S3].

Phases the rebate out for higher incomes — reduced by 5% of income above $75,000 (single), $112,500 (head of household), or $150,000 (joint) — concentrating the benefit on middle- and lower-income households [S3].
Applies retroactively to calendar quarters ending after December 31, 2021, capturing the record profits of 2022, with 2022 rebates required to be paid by June 30, 2023 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers and importers — companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day, which aggregates affiliated companies together for the threshold [S2][S3]. They would owe the tax on oil sold above pre-pandemic benchmark prices, retroactive into 2022.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large crude oil producers and importers

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied per barrel of crude, so companies could pass part of it through to consumers at the pump, raising gasoline prices at exactly the moments when prices are already spiking [S3].

The tax only applies to profits above the 2015-2019 average Brent price, so it does nothing about high-but-below-benchmark prices, and the 300,000-barrel threshold plus aggregation rules leave smaller producers entirely untouched [S3].
Applying the tax retroactively to 2022 quarters raises legal and fairness concerns about taxing conduct after the fact, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the rebate outweighs any likely pass-through at the pump, since the credit is refundable, capped at the amount collected, and phases out only at higher incomes. The design risks are real but narrow: the per-barrel structure invites some pass-through to gas prices, and the benchmark trigger means the tax only bites during exceptional price spikes. Weighing the two, the bill is a straightforward transfer from large oil companies' excess profits to ordinary taxpayers, with design flaws rather than fundamental ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on February 14, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The bill's only action in its two years in Congress was that referral; no markup, no subcommittee action, no floor vote is recorded in its action history [S5].
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
The bill would have applied retroactively to 2022, when oil prices spiked after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and large producers recorded record profits [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large crude oil producers and importers are better off: they never faced the 50% windfall tax or the retroactive charge on their 2022 profits, because the Ways and Means Committee never brought the bill up.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 House Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or any further action in the two years after its referral.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill before the committee for a markup or vote.

against.name: Major oil companies and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed windfall profits taxes on oil producers as a penalty on investment during the 2022 price spike.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters (the sponsor plus 18 cosponsors) were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never brought it to a vote.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: The bill would tax 50% of their profits above pre-pandemic benchmark prices, retroactive into 2022, hitting companies handling more than 300,000 barrels a day. Their interest in blocking it ran against the rebate ordinary households would have received from the same money.
The 300,000-barrel daily threshold and aggregation rules exempt smaller producers from the tax entirely, so the burden falls only on the largest firms.
